concepts.statement_en: In fictional Barangay Maligaya, riverside homes flood; one household needs evacuation help and a school may serve as shelter but has not been confirmed.
Mark the flood hazard, people who may need help, and possible routes and resources. Record uncertainties. Ask the local DRRM office and health team to verify the map before use.
The practice map is not an official hazard map or evacuation order. Use official assessments and protect household privacy.
Heavy rain is forecast. Nena’s family asks when and where to evacuate, but the printed directory is old.

Read the current official warning and confirm the evacuation order, safe route, accessible shelter and contact with the barangay DRRM focal person. Relay only the verified message, recording its time and source.
Do not invent an evacuation order, give an unverified hotline or direct people along an unconfirmed route. Follow local authority and updates.
Pio’s family is making a go-bag or e-balde. They have an infant and a member taking regular medicine; money is limited and the container must be easy to carry.

Use a current DOH and local checklist. Prioritize safe water, food, light, communication, basic hygiene, water-protected documents and first-aid supplies. Include personal medicines and infant needs under the family’s care plan; check expiry and portability.
Items are examples, not a mandatory universal list or permission to dispense medicines. Adapt to local hazards, household needs and medical plans.
After flooding, a BHW is asked to record concerns and relay information to a response team. It is unclear whether an old BHERT roster is active.

Confirm the current team, role, lead and reporting channel with the barangay and health supervisor. Report the minimum needed: location, hazard, urgent need, action taken and next contact. Hand over and record time; protect sensitive details.
The old pandemic-era BHERT slide does not establish today’s team composition, isolation or contact-tracing mandate. Do not assign clinical or enforcement duties to a BHW.
At a temporary shelter, a child may lack food, safe water is limited, a resident needs regular medicine, and another is distressed.

Identify and link four domains: medical/public health, nutrition, safe water/sanitation/hygiene (WASH), and mental health/psychosocial support (MHPSS). Alert assigned staff to urgent risk and interrupted services. For a distressed person, check safety, listen with consent, and link to practical help and qualified support.
Recognizing a domain does not authorize prescribing, ration-setting, declaring water safe or providing therapy. Follow local clinical and service protocols.
In a fictional tabletop, flooding and an evacuation advisory coincide. A family needs help leaving, a resident’s medicine is running low, shelter water is uncertain and a volunteer is exhausted.

Check the official warning and local plan. Identify confirmed contacts for evacuation, clinical continuity, WASH and psychosocial support. Report immediate risk to the right team, confirm handover, and set follow-up. A responder should rest and seek support when it is unsafe to continue.
This is a tabletop only. It does not replace official incident command, clinical assessment, water testing or a live drill. Verify every contact and route before use.
